questions.q: $\sum_{k=1}^5 \frac{1^3+2^3+\ldots+k^3}{1+3+5+\ldots+(2 k-1)}$ is equal to
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \sum_{k=1}^5 \frac{1^3+2^3+\ldots+k^3}{1+3+5+\ldots .+(2 k-1)} \\ & =\sum_{k=1}^5 \frac{\left(\frac{k(k+1)}{2}\right)^2}{k^2} \\ & \qquad\left[\begin{array}{l}\because n^3=\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2 \\ \text { and } 1+3+5 \ldots+(2 K-1)=K^2\end{array}\right] \\ & =\sum_{k=1}^5 \frac{(k+1)^2}{4}=\frac{2^2+3^2+4^2+5^2+6^2}{4} \\ & =\frac{4+9+16+25+36}{4}=\frac{90}{4}=22.5\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $a, b$ and $c$ form a geometric progression with common ratio $r$, then the sum of the ordinates of the points of intersection of the line $a x+b y+c=0$ and the curve $x+2 y^2=0$ is
questions.solution:
Since, $a, b$ and $c$ form a geometric progression
$\therefore \quad a=a, b=a r, c=a r^2$
Therefore, given line becomes
$\begin{aligned} & a x+a r y+a r^2 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & x+r y+r^2 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow & x & =-r y-r^2\end{aligned}$
On putting $x=-r y-r^2$ in given curve $x+2 y^2=0$, we get
$\begin{aligned}-r y-r^2+2 y^2 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad 2 y^2-r y-r^2 & =0\end{aligned}\therefore$ Sum of ordinates $=\frac{r}{2}$

questions.q: If $x+y=60, x>0, y>0$, then the maximum value of $x y^3$ is
questions.solution: Given, $x+y=60$ By $\mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM}\begin{array}{ll}$& $\frac{x+\frac{y}{3}+\frac{y}{3}+\frac{y}{3}}{4} \geq\left(\frac{x y^3}{27}\right)^{1 / 4}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & $\frac{x+y}{4} \geq\left(\frac{x y^3}{27}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & $\frac{60}{4} \geq\left(\frac{x y^3}{27}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & $\frac{x y^3}{27} \leq($15)^4 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & x y³ \leq 3^3 $\times$3^4 $\times$5^4 \Rightarrow x y³ \leq $\frac{(45)^4}{3} \end{array}\therefore$ Maximum value of $x y^3$ is $\frac{(45)^4}{3}$.

questions.q: $\theta$ and $\alpha$ lie in $Q_3$. If $\cos (\theta-\alpha), \cos \theta, \cos (\theta+\alpha)$ are in harmonic progression, then $\cos \theta \sec \frac{\alpha}{2}=$
questions.solution: Given, $\cos (\theta-\alpha), \cos \theta, \cos (\theta+\alpha)$ are in HP $\begin{array}{lc}\because & \frac{2}{\cos \theta}=\frac{1}{\cos (\theta-\alpha)}+\frac{1}{\cos (\theta+\alpha)}\\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2}{\cos \theta}=\frac{\cos (\theta+\alpha)+\cos (\theta-\alpha)}{\cos (\theta-\alpha) \cos (\theta+\alpha)}\\ \Rightarrow & \frac{2}{\cos \theta}=\frac{2 \cos \theta \cos \alpha}{\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \alpha}\\ \Rightarrow & \cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 $\alpha=\cos ^2 $\theta \cos \alpha\\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \cos ^2 \theta(1-\cos \alpha)=\sin ^2 $\alpha\\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \cos ^2 \$theta=\frac{1-\cos 2 \alpha}{1-\cos ^2 \alpha}=$1+\cos \alpha\\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \cos ^2 \theta=2 \cos ^2 $\frac{\alpha}{2} \Rightarrow \cos \theta \sec \alpha$/ $2=\sqrt{2}\end{array}

questions.q: The period of $\tan k y+\sin k y$, where $k=1+4+9+\ldots 20$ terms, is
questions.solution: $k=1+4+9+\ldots$ upto 20 terms $\begin{aligned}$& \therefore k=$\sum$n^2=$\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}, \text { where }$n=20 \\ & \therefore k=$\frac{20 \times 21 \times 41}{6}=$70 $\times$41=2870 \end{aligned} $\therefore$ Period of tan $k y$ is $\frac{2 \pi}{2870}$ and period of $\sin k y$ is $\frac{2 \pi}{2870}$ i.e. $\frac{\pi}{1435}$ \therefore $\text { Required period }=\frac{\pi}{1435}$

questions.q: If the roots of $x^5-a x^4+b x^3-c x^2+d x-1=0$ are all positive such that their arithmetic mean and geometric mean are equal, then $a+b+c+d=$
questions.solution: Given equation is $x^5-a x^4+b x-c x+d x-1=0$. Here, geometrical mean and arithmetic mean are equal then all the roots are equal. Let $\alpha$ is the root of the equation. $\frac{\alpha+\alpha+\alpha+\alpha+\alpha}{5}=\left(\alpha^5\right)^{1 / 5}$ Here, sum of all roots is $a$. $\begin{gathered} \frac{a}{5}=\alpha \\ a=5 \alpha \end{gathered}(\alpha \alpha \alpha \alpha \alpha)^{1 / 5}=\frac{-e}{a}=-(-1)=1\begin{aligned} & \alpha^{5 \times \frac{1}{5}}=1 \\ & \alpha=1 \end{aligned}$ From (i), $a=5$. Now, $\begin{aligned} & \alpha \alpha+\alpha \alpha+\alpha \alpha+\ldots . .+\alpha \alpha(10 \text { times })=b \\ & 10 \alpha^2=b \\ & b=10 \\ & \alpha \alpha \alpha+\alpha \alpha \alpha+\ldots . .+10 \text { times }=c \\ & 10 \alpha^3=c \\ & c=10 \\ & \alpha \alpha \alpha \alpha+\alpha \alpha \alpha \alpha+\ldots \ldots \ldots+5 \text { times }=d \\ & 5 \alpha^4=d \\ & d=5 \end{aligned}$ Therefore, $a+d+c+b=5+5+10+10=30$.

questions.q: For a real variable $a>1$, consider the points $A_k=\left(k a, a^k\right), k=1,2, \ldots ., n$ in the Cartesian plane. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ represent respectively the arithmetic mean of $x$-coordinates and the geometric mean of $y$ coordinates of $A_k$, then the locus of the point $P(\alpha, \beta)$ is
questions.solution: We have, $\begin{aligned} \alpha & =\frac{a+2 a+3 a+\ldots+n a}{n} \\ & =\frac{a[1+2+3+\ldots+n]}{n} \\ & =\frac{a n(n+1)}{2 n}=\frac{a(n+1)}{2}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \text { and } \beta=\left(a \cdot a^2 \cdot a^3 \cdot a^4 \ldots a^n\right)^{1 / n} \\ & \qquad=\left(a^{1+2+3+\ldots n}\right)^{1 / n}=a^{\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^{1 / n}}=a^{\frac{n+1}{2}} \\ & \text { Now, } \beta^2=a^{n+1} \\ & \text { and }\left(\frac{2 \alpha}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}=\left(\frac{2 a(n+1)}{2(n+1)}\right)^{n+1}=a^{n+1} \\ & \therefore \quad \beta^2=\left(\frac{2 \alpha}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}\end{aligned}$ So, locus of point $P(\alpha, \beta)$ is $y^2=\left(\frac{2 x}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}$

questions.q: If the roots of the equation, $8 x^3+6 p x^2+3 q x-27=0$ are in a geometric progression, then $q^2+9 p^2+6 p q+q / p=$
questions.solution: Let roots of the equation $8 x^3+6 p x^2+3 q x-27=0 \text { are } \frac{a}{r}, a, \text { ar. }\therefore \quad \frac{a}{r}+a+a r=\frac{-6 p}{8}=\frac{-3 p}{4}\Rightarrow \quad a\left(\frac{1}{r}+1+r\right)=\frac{-3 p}{4}\ldots$ (i) \left(\frac{a}{r} \cdot a\right)+(a \cdot a r)+\left(\frac{a}{r} \cdot a r\right)=\frac{3 q}{8}\Rightarrow \quad a^2\left(\frac{1}{r}+r+1\right)=\frac{3 q}{8}\ldots$ (ii) and $\quad \frac{a}{r} \times a \times a r=\frac{27}{8}\Rightarrow \quad a^3=\frac{27}{8} \Rightarrow a=\frac{3}{2}\ldots$ (iii) From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $a=\frac{3 q / 8}{-3 p / 4}=-\frac{q}{2 p}\ldots$ (iv) From Eqs. (iii)and (iv), we have $\frac{-q}{2 p}=\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow-q=3 p$ Now, $\quad q^2+9 p^2+6 p q+\frac{q}{p}\Rightarrow \quad 9 p^2+9 p^2+6 p(-3 p)+\frac{(-3 p)}{p}\Rightarrow \quad 18 p^2-18 p^2-3=-3

(i)$ Also, $\begin{aligned} & \tan ^{-1} x, \tan ^{-1} y, \tan ^{-1} z \text { are in A.P. } \\ \therefore \quad & 2 \tan ^{-1} y=\tan ^{-1} x+\tan ^{-1} z \\ & \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 y}{1-y^2}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x+z}{1-x z}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2 y}{1-y^2}=\frac{x+z}{1-x z} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2 y}{1-y^2}=\frac{2 y}{1-x z}... [From (i)] \\ & \Rightarrow 1-y^2=1-x z \\ & \Rightarrow y^2=x z \end{aligned}\therefore \quad x, y, \mathrm{z} \text { are in G.P. }... (ii)$ From (i) and (ii), we get $x=y=\mathrm{z}$

questions.q: In a harmonic progression ${t}_{1}, {t}_{2}, {t}_{3}, \ldots \ldots \ldots . . ,$ it is given that ${t}_{5} = 20$ and ${t}_{6} = 50.$ If ${S}_{n}$ denotes the sum of first $n$ terms of this, then the value of $n$ for which ${S}_{n}$ is maximum is
questions.solution:
Let the first term be $a$ and the common difference be $d$, then

$20 = \dfrac{1}{a + 4d}$ and $50 = \dfrac{1}{a + 5d}$
On solving, we get,

$d = - \dfrac{3}{100}$ and $a = \dfrac{17}{100}$
Hence, ${t}_{r} = \dfrac{100}{20 - 3r} > 0 ⇒ r < \dfrac{20}{3} ⇒ {r}_\max = 6$
So, sum is maximum for $n = 6,$ as after this terms are negative

questions.q: If $x, y$ are positive real numbers and $3x + 4y = 5,$ then the largest possible value of $16{x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ is
questions.solution:
$2\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right) + 3\left(\dfrac{4y}{3}\right) = 5$
$\dfrac{3x}{2} + \dfrac{3x}{2} + \dfrac{4y}{3} + \dfrac{4y}{3} + \dfrac{4y}{3} = 5$
Using $A . M \ge G . M$ for $\dfrac{3x}{2}, \dfrac{3x}{2}, \dfrac{4y}{3}, \dfrac{4y}{3}, \dfrac{4y}{3}$
$\dfrac{\dfrac{3x}{2} + \dfrac{3x}{2} + \dfrac{4y}{3} + \dfrac{4y}{3} + \dfrac{4y}{3}}{5} \ge {\left({\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{4y}{3}\right)}^{3}\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{5}}$
$\dfrac{3x + 4y}{5} \ge {\left(\dfrac{{3}^{2}{4}^{3}}{{2}^{2}{3}^{3}}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{5}}$
$1 \ge {\left(\dfrac{{2}^{4}}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{5}}$
$16{x}^{2}{y}^{3} \le 3$
Maximum value of $16{x}^{2}{y}^{3} = 3$

questions.q: If $x, \left|x + 1\right|$ and \left|x - 1\right|$ are the first three terms of an arithmetic progression, then its sum upto $20$ terms is$
questions.solution:
$2\left|x + 1\right| = x + \left|x - 1\right|$
(i) Case- $Ι$ :-

$x \le - 1$
$2\left(- x - 1\right) = x + \left(- x + 1\right) ⇒ - 2x - 2 = 1$
$⇒ x = - \dfrac{3}{2}$
Then the A.P. is $\to - \dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2} . . . . . .$
${S}_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}\left[- 3 + 19 \times 2\right] = \dfrac{20}{2} \times 35 = 350$
(ii) Case- $ΙΙ$ :-
$- 1 \le x < 1$
$2\left(x + 1\right) = x + \left(- x + 1\right) ⇒ 2x + 2 = 1 ⇒ x = - \dfrac{1}{2}$
Then the A.P. is $\to - \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{3}{2} . . . . . .$
${S}_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}\left[- 1 + 19 \times 1\right] = 10 \times 18 = 180$
(ii) Case- $ΙΙΙ$ :-
$x \ge 1$
$2\left(x + 1\right) = x + x - 1 ⇒ 2x + 2 = 2x - 1 ⇒ 2 = - 1$
(not possible)
Hence, the required sum is $350$ or $180$
questions.source: 99 Percentile Qs Bank for JEE Main

questions.q: If $2, 7, 9$ and $5$ are subtracted respectively from four numbers in geometric progression, then the resulting numbers are in arithmetic progression. The smallest of the four numbers is
questions.solution:
Let the numbers be $\text{a}, \text{ar}, {\text{ar}}^{\text{2}}, {\text{ar}}^{\text{3}}$ ,
$⇒ a - 2, ar - 7, ar^{2} - 9$ and $ar^{3} - 5$ are in $A . P .$
$⇒ \left(a - 2\right) + \left($ar^{2} - 9\right) = $2\left($ar - 7\right)$ and \left(ar - 7\right) + \left(ar^{3} - 5\right) = 2\left(ar^{2} - 9\right)$
$⇒ a + ar^{2} = 2ar - 3$ and $ar + ar^{3} = 2ar^{2} - 6$
$⇒ 1 + r^{2} = 2r - \dfrac{3}{a}$and $1 + r^{2} = 2r - \dfrac{6}{ar}$
$⇒ \dfrac{3}{a} = \dfrac{6}{ar}⇒ r = 2$
$⇒ \dfrac{3}{a} =2r - 1 - r^{2} = 4 - 1 - 4 = - 1 ⇒ a = - 3$
So, the numbers are $– 3, – 6, – 12, – 24$

questions.q: If the roots of the equation $16 x^3-44 x^2+36 x-9=0$ are in harmonic progression, then its greatest root is
questions.solution: The given equation is $16 x^3-44 x^2+36 x-9=0$ Let $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$ are in H.P. $\Rightarrow \frac{3}{\beta}=\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\beta} \Rightarrow \frac{3}{\beta}=\frac{\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha}{\alpha \gamma \beta}\Rightarrow \frac{3}{\beta}=\frac{36 / 16}{9 / 16}=4 \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{3}{4}$ Now, $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{11}{4} \Rightarrow \alpha+\gamma=\frac{11}{4}-\frac{3}{4}=2$ ...(i) And $\alpha \beta \gamma=\frac{9}{16} \Rightarrow \alpha \gamma=\frac{9}{16} \times \frac{4}{3}=\frac{3}{4}$...(ii) Solving eqn. (i) and (ii) : $\alpha=\frac{3}{2}, \gamma=\frac{1}{2}\therefore$ Greatest root is $\alpha=\frac{3}{2}$.

questions.q: $p, x_1, x_2 \ldots, x_n$ and $q, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_{\mathrm{n}}$ are two arithmetic progressions with common differences a and $\mathrm{b}$ respectively. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the arithmetic means of $x_1, x_2, \ldots x_n$, and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ respectively. Then the locus of $P(\alpha, \beta)$ is
questions.solution:
It is given that $p, x_1, x_2, x_3 \ldots x_n$ and $q, y_1, y_2, y_3 \ldots y_n$ are in A.P. whose common difference are $a$ and $b$ respectively. $\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad$x_1 & =p+a, x_n=p+n a \\ y_1 & =q+b, y_n=q+n b \end{aligned} Also, given $\alpha$ is A.M. of $x_1, x_2, x_3 \ldots x_n\begin{array}{rlrl} \therefore$& $\alpha$& =$\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3+\ldots .+x_n}{n}$\\ \Rightarrow & $\alpha=\frac{n}{2} \frac{\left(x_1+x_n\right)}{n}$\\ \Rightarrow & $\alpha=\frac{x_1+x_n}{2} \end{array}$Similarly, $\beta$ is A.M. of $y_1, y_2, y_3 \ldots y_n$. So, $\beta=\frac{y_1+y_n}{2}$Thus, substituting the value of $x, x_n, y$ and $y_n$, we get
From Eqs. $(i)$ and (ii) eliminate $(n+1)$, we get $\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{2 \alpha-2 p}{a}=\frac{2 \beta-2 q}{b}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & b($\alpha-$p)=a($\beta-$q) \end{aligned} Hence, locus of $p(\alpha, \beta)$ is $b(x-p)=a(y-q)$

questions.q: Let \(P(n): 1^2+2^2+3^2+\ldots+n²\) \(=$\frac{6(n-1)(n-2) \ldots(n-2020)+2 n^3+3 n^2+n}{6}$\), for all \(n \in \mathbf{N}\). Then which of the following is correct?
options: \(P(n)\) is not true for any \(n \in N\)
questions.solution: Given statement \(\begin{aligned} \text{ and } P(n)=1^2+2^2+3^2+\ldots+n²= \\ \text{ and } \frac{6(n-1)(n-2) \ldots(n-2020)+2 n³+3 n²+n}{6} \end{aligned}\) \(\because\) We know that, \$(\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } 1^2+2^2+3^2+\ldots+n²=$\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}$\\ \text{ and } \therefore \quad $\frac{6(n-1)(n-2) \ldots(n-2020)+2 n^3+3 n^2+n}{6}$\\ \text{ and } \quad=(n-1)(n-2) \ldots(n-2020)+$\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6} \end{aligned}$\) will be \($\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}$\) if \(n=1,2,3, \ldots ., 2020\) only. Therefore, \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \leq 2020\). Hence, option (c) is correct.$

questions.q: Let \(A, G, H\) and \(S\) respectively denote the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, harmonic mean and the sum of the numbers \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n\). Then the value of \(x\) at which the function \(f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n\left($x-a_k\right)^2\) has minimum is$
questions.solution: Given function \(f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n\left($x-a_k\right)^2\) \(=\sum_{k=1}^n\left($x^2-2 x a_k+a_k^2\right)\) \(\begin{aligned} \text{ and } =n x²-2 x\left($a_1+a_2+a_3+\ldots a_n\right) \\ \text{ and } +\left($a_1^2+a_2^2+\ldots+a_n^2\right) \end{aligned}\) \(\because\) The quadratic expression \(a x²+b x+c\) has its minimum value at \(x=-\frac{b}{2 a}\). \(\therefore f(x)\) has it's minimum value at \$(\begin{aligned}$ \text{ and } x=-$\frac{-2\left(a_1+a_2+a_3+\ldots+a_n\right)}{2 n}$\\ \text{ and } =$\frac{a_1+a_2+a_3+\ldots+a_n}{n} \Rightarrow$x=A \end{aligned}\) Hence, option (4) is correct.$

questions.q: $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h$ be distinct elements in the set $\{-7,-5,-3,-2,2,4,6,13\}$. The minimum value of $(a+b+c+d)^2+(e+f+g+h)^2$ is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned}$& $\text { Let }$a+b+c+d=x $\text { and }$e+f+g+h=y \\ & x²+y²=(x+y)^2-2 x y \\ & =(13+6+4+2-2-3-5-7)^2-2 x y \\ & =64-2 x y \end{aligned} As we know $\mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM}\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{x+y}{2} \geq \sqrt{x y}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & $\frac{8}{2} \geq \sqrt{x y}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & x y \leq 16 \end{aligned} $x^2+y^2$ is minimum when $x y$ is maximum. The maximum value of $x y=16$. The minimum value of $x^2+y^2=64-2 \times 16=32\therefore$ The minimum values of (a+b+c+d)^2+(e+f+g+h)=32

questions.q: If AM of two numbers is twice of their GM, then the ratio of greatest number to smallest number is
questions.solution:
Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$

Since, $\dfrac{x + y}{2} = 2\sqrt{xy}$

$⇒ x + y = 4\sqrt{xy}$ .....(i)

$⇒ {\left(x + y\right)}^{2} = 16xy$

Also ${\left(x - y\right)}^{2} = {\left(x + y\right)}^{2} - 4xy$

$∴ {\left(x - y\right)}^{2} = 16xy - 4xy = 12xy$

$⇒ x - y = 2\sqrt{3xy}$ ...(ii)

On solving Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$x = ( 2 + \sqrt{3} ) \sqrt{xy}$

and $y = ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) \sqrt{xy}$

$∴$ Required ratio = $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{( 2 + \sqrt{3} ) \sqrt{xy}}{( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) \sqrt{xy}}$

$= {\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)}^{2} = 7 + 4\sqrt{3}$

and~$2y = tan$\dfrac{π}{9} +$tan$\dfrac{5\pi}{18}

$= \left|cot\dfrac{2\pi}{9} --cot\dfrac{2\pi}{9}\right| =0$

\left(astan \dfrac{5\pi}{18} ==cot\dfrac{2\pi}{9}$; $tan\dfrac{7\pi}{18} ==cot\dfrac{π}{9}\right)

questions.q:
The smallest possible value of $p + q + r$ (where $p > 6$), if \left(1 + 3 + 5 + . . . + p\right) + \left(1 + 3 + 5 + . . . + q\right) = \left(1 + 3 + 5 + . . . + r\right)$ where each set of parentheses contains the sum of consecutive odd integers as shown.

$
questions.solution:
We know that 1 + 3 + 5 + .... + (2k - 1) $= k^{2}$

Thus, the given equation can be written as ${\left(\dfrac{p + 1}{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{q + 1}{2}\right)}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{r + 1}{2}\right)}^{2} ⇒ {\left(p + 1\right)}^{2} + { \left(q + 1\right)}^{2} = { \left($r + 1\right)}^{2}$

Therefore, \left($p + 1, q + 1, r + 1\right)$ forms a Pythagoren triple. As $p > 6, p + 1 > 7$ .

The first Pythagorean triple containing a number > 7 is (6, 8, 10).

We may take p + 1 = 8, q + 1 = 6, r + 1 = 10 $⇒ p + q + r = 21$

questions.q: In an arithmetic progression the ${\left(p + 1\right)}^{th}$ term is twice the ${\left(q + 1\right)}^{th}$ term. If its ${\left(3p + 1\right)}^{th}$ term is $\lambda$ times the ${\left(p + q + 1\right)}^{th}$ term, then $\lambda$ is equal to
questions.solution:
For the A.P. let $a$ be the first term and $d$ be the common difference

Given ${T}_{p + 1} = 2{T}_{q + 1}$
$⇒ a + pd = 2\left(a + qd\right) ⇒ a = \left(p - 2q\right)d$
Also,
${T}_{3p + 1} = \lambda{T}_{p + q + 1}$
$a + 3pd = \lambda \left(a + \left($p + q\right)d\right)$
$a \left(\lambda -$1\right) = d \left($3p - \lambdap - \lambdaq\right)$
So, \left($p - 2q\right)d = $\dfrac{\left(\lambdap + \lambdaq - 3p\right)d}{1 - \lambda}
$⇒ p - p\lambda - 2q + 2q\lambda = \lambdap + \lambdaq - 3p$
$⇒ \lambda\left(p + q + p - 2q\right) = p - 2q + 3p$
$⇒ \lambda = $\dfrac{4p - 2q}{2p - q} = \dfrac{2\left(2p - q\right)}{2p - q} =$2$

$

B. If a,b,c are three consecutive terms of a progression such that \left(\dfrac{a - b}{b - c}\right) = \dfrac{a}$ then a, b, c are in Q. G.P.
C. If a, b, c are in A.P. then ${2}^{ax + 1}, {2}^{bx + 1}, {2}^{cx + 1} ( x \ne 0 )$ are in R. H.P.
D. If $- 1 < a, b, c < 1$ & a, b, c are in A.P. & $x = ( \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}a^{n} ) + 1, y = ( \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}b^{n} ) + 1, z = ( \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}c^{n} ) + 1$ then $\dfrac{1}{x}, \dfrac{1}{y}, \dfrac{1}{z}$ are in S. A.G.P.
T. None
$
options: $A \to R; B \to R; C \to Q; D \to P$
$A \to P; B \to Q; C \to R; D \to S$
$A \to R; B \to Q; C \to R; D \to P$
$A \to Q; B \to S; C \to P; D \to Q$

A. we have

$\log_{\mathrm{ex}} ⁡ e, \log_{\mathrm{ey}} ⁡ e, \log_{\mathrm{ez}} ⁡ e$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{1 + lnx}, \dfrac{1}{1 + lny}, \dfrac{1}{1 + lnz}$

~

B. $\dfrac{a - b}{b - c} = \dfrac{a}{c}$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{2ac}{a + c}$

$⇒ a, b, careinH . P .$

~

C. Since~$a, b, c$~are in AP

~ ~ & $b - a = c - b = d$(say)

$⇒ {2}^{ax + 1}, {2}^{bx + 1}, {2}^{cx + 1}$~will be in GP.

as~$\dfrac{2bx + 1}{2ax + 1} = \dfrac{{2}^{cx + 1}}{2bx + 1} = {2}^{dx} \left(constant\right)$

D.~ ~Using the formula of the sum of an infinite GP

~ \text{ and } \text{ and } $x = $\dfrac{1}{1 - a}$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{x} =$1 - a$
and~
~ ~ \text{ and } $y = $\dfrac{1}{1 - b}$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{y} =$1 - b$ ,
and
~ ~ ~ \text{ and } \text{ and } $z = $\dfrac{1}{1 - c}$⇒ $\dfrac{1}{z} =$1 - c$

Since~$a, b, c$~are in AP

$⇒ 1 - a, 1 - b, 1 - c$~are also in AP

Hence \dfrac{1}{x}, \dfrac{1}{y}, \dfrac{1}{z}$areinA . P .

questions.q: If $11$ arithmetic means are inserted between $28$ and $10,$ then the number of integral arithmetic means are
questions.solution:
Let, ${A}_{1}, {A}_{2}, {A}_{3}, \ldots \ldots , {A}_{11}$ be $11$ A.M.’s between $28$ and $10$
$⇒ 28, {A}_{1}, {A}_{2}, \ldots \ldots , {A}_{11}, 10$ are in A.P

Let, $d$ be the common difference of A.P.
Also, the number of terms $= 13$

$⇒ 10 = {T}_{13} = {T}_{1} + 12d = 28 + 12d$
$⇒ d = \dfrac{10 - 28}{12} = \dfrac{- 18}{12} = \dfrac{- 3}{2}$
$⇒$ Number of integral A.M.’s are $5$

questions.q: $\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}\dfrac{r}{r^{4} + r^{2} + 1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let, $Ι\left(r\right) = \dfrac{r}{r^{4} + r^{2} + 1} = \dfrac{r}{\left(r^{2} + r + 1\right)\left(r^{2} - r + 1\right)}$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left\{\dfrac{\left(r^{2} + r + 1\right) - \left(r^{2} - r + 1\right)}{\left(r^{2} + r + 1\right)\left(r^{2} - r + 1\right)}\right\}$
$= - \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{r^{2} + r + 1} - \dfrac{1}{r^{2} - r + 1}\right)
$= - $\dfrac{1}{2} \left(V \left(r\right) - V \left(r - 1\right)\right)$
$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}Ι \left(r\right) = - $\dfrac{1}{2}\left($V \left($n\right) - $V\left($0\right)\right)$
$= - $\dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2} + n + 1} -$1\right)$
$= $\dfrac{1}{2}\left($1 - $\dfrac{1}{n^{2} + n + 1}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\left(n^{2} + n\right)}{\left(n^{2} + n + 1\right)}$

questions.q: The sum of the ${3}^{rd}$ and the ${4}^{th}$ terms of a $G . P .$ is $60$ and the product of its first three terms is $1000.$ If the first term of this $G . P .$ is positive, then its ${7}^{th}$ term is:
questions.solution:
Let the $' G . P . '$~be

$\dfrac{a}{r}, a, ar, ar^{2}$

Given,~

$\dfrac{a}{r} \cdot a \cdot ar = 1000$

$⇒ a^{3} = 1000$

$⇒ a = 10$

Also, $ar + ar^{2} = 60$

$⇒ 10\left(r + r^{2}\right) = 60$

$⇒ r + r^{2} = 6$

$⇒ r^{2} + r - 6 = 0$

$⇒ \left(r - 2\right)\left(r + 3\right) = 0$

So,~$r = 2$ or $r = - 3$

As ${1}^{st}$ term~is positive $∴ r = 2$

$∴ G . P .$ is $' 5 ' , ' 10 ' , ' 20 ' . . . . . . .$

Hence,~${7}^{th}$~term is~$5 \cdot \left(2\right)6 = 320 .$
